title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 326
paragraphs: Now after Sesostris had ended his life, his son Pheros, they told me, received the kingdom in succession; and he made no warlike expedition, but it chanced to him to become blind by reason of the following accident. When the river had come down in flood, rising to a height of eighteen cubits (higher than ever before), and had gone over the fields, a wind fell upon it and the river became agitated by waves; and this king (they say), moved by presumptuous folly, took a spear and cast it into the midst of the eddies of the stream; and immediately upon this he had a disease of the eyes and was by it made blind. For ten years, then, he was blind, and in the eleventh year there came to him an oracle from the city of Buto, saying that the time of his punishment had expired, and that he should see again if he washed his eyes with the water of a woman who had lain only with her own husband and had not known other men. First he made trial of his own wife, and then, as he continued blind, he went on to try all the women in turn; and when he had at last regained his sight, he gathered together all the women with whom he had made the trial (except her by whose means he had regained his sight) into one city, which is now named Erythrabolus, and having gathered them there he consumed them all by fire, as well as the city itself. As for her by whose means he had regained his sight, he had her himself to wife. Then, after he had escaped the malady of his eyes, he dedicated offerings at each of the temples of renown, and especially (to mention only the most worthy of mention) he dedicated at the temple of the Sun works that are worth seeing — namely two obelisks of stone, each of a single block, measuring a hundred cubits each in length and eight cubits in breadth.
